1Where are restrooms needed?

* has a Throne restroom. More districts under "Districts and your own data" below.

A need tier says how badly a block needs a public restroom, from 1 (least) to 5 (most). Blocks within a 5-minute walk of an open restroom are served and get no tier. For every other block FLUSHING asks four questions: how many people walk by, how many residents are older, very young or disabled, how many are in poverty, and how often public urination is reported. Each answer is rated 1 to 5, and the block takes its highest rating, as DOT staff described their Pedestrian Demand Map: one strong reason is enough to set a street's class. Click any block to see which question set it.

What sets the tier

Most people can leave this on the default. Foot traffic follows DOT's street classes (Global 5, Regional 4, Neighborhood 3, Community 2, Baseline 1). Subway follows DOT's own rule: a station within 150 m with more than 50,000 riders a week (about 7,100 a day) makes it Regional (4); any other station, Neighborhood (3). Subway entries are in thousands a day; blank means none. v3's own cut-offs are the "v3" preset. Resident and poverty cut-offs are round numbers, the same in every district (see Numbers). "Equity first" lowers them; "Foot traffic first" caps them at tier 3. The 30-site list and the Throne check always use the default.

Walk and contract assumptions

The walk standard and speed decide who is served. The other three only estimate visits and cost for contracts; they do not change tiers. The share is an assumption until the city publishes Throne's New York use counts; the best public data are from Throne's Long Beach, California pilot, where the busiest unit averaged 119 uses a day. Cost is the Throne pilot: $4M for 17 units for a year, units and service together. Speed is 3.5 ft a second, the walking speed US signal timing uses (MUTCD 4E.06); a brisk adult is about 80. The detour factor turns a straight line into a street walk: on a perfect grid it averages 4/π ≈ 1.27. Sources for every number: Numbers.

Which restrooms count

Click any restroom on the map to stop counting it.

2Where can they go?

Choose the land a unit may stand on. Land never changes a block's tier; it only decides where a unit is allowed. Each candidate then gets a desk review modelled on DOT's siting steps: what the data can check, what needs a site visit, and who must approve.

3Where should they go?

FLUSHING puts a unit on the highest-tier allowed block (ties go to the most people on foot), counts it as open, re-sorts every block and repeats, so units spread out instead of stacking up. Each pick shows its site check and a suggested type of restroom.

Or see the reference list in our memo: the next 30 sites to consider across the loaded districts, always on the default settings.

Key terms
Need tier
How badly a block needs a public restroom: 1 (least) to 5 (most). Four questions each give a rating from 1 to 5; the block takes the highest. Nothing is weighted or added. Served blocks get no tier.
Served · partly served · gap
Served: an open restroom within a 5-minute walk; not ranked. Partly served: 5 to 10 minutes; the tier is lowered by one. Gap: beyond 10 minutes.
Deciding factor
The one factor that set the block's tier. Ties between blocks go to more people on foot, then more residents.
Foot traffic
DOT's five street classes (Global, Regional, Neighborhood, Community, Baseline), or a subway station within 150 m with many daily entries.
Vulnerable residents
Share of residents aged 65+, under 5, or under 65 with a disability (Census survey). A block within a 10-minute walk of a homeless drop-in centre counts as at least tier 4. Resident factors only count on blocks with 10 or more residents.
Poverty · complaints
Poverty rate (Census survey) and yearly 311 public-urination complaints within 200 m.
Walk
Straight-line distance × 1.3 for real streets, at 64 m a minute, a slower walker's pace.
Clear path
The open sidewalk left beside a unit. DOT's Street Design Manual asks for 8 ft in front of an automatic toilet (6 ft 7 in wide) and 5 ft on its other sides, so a sidewalk unit needs about 15 ft, or about 20 ft if the 5 ft applies at the curb. The tool checks the widest sidewalk on the block, not the exact spot.
Lens
A view for one team (Coverage, Evening & winter, Zoning & BIDs, Maintenance & contracts, Co-location & contacts). It never changes a tier; it adds layers and a results panel.
Service ring
A loop one cleaning crew drives, through several units and, where there is one, a Parks restroom as its base.
Desk review · site visit
The tool checks what public data can show. Sun, curb uses, below-grade structures and lighting need someone on site.
Visits a day
1% of people on foot, up to 120, for people with no restroom nearby. Used for cleaning schedules and cost, never for ranking.
Data and sources
  • Restrooms: NYC Public Restrooms (open data) and the 17 announced Throne units
  • Foot traffic: DOT Pedestrian Mobility Plan street classes; MTA subway ridership
  • Residents: 2020 Census blocks; Census survey (ACS) for age, disability and poverty
  • Complaints: 311 service requests (public urination)
  • Land: MapPLUTO tax lots, parks and plazas; sidewalk widths from city planimetrics

About

This is a prototype sandbox. It was built to test an idea and to be picked apart. The numbers are rough estimates. Nothing here should be used to choose a site without checking it on the ground.

FLUSHING answers three questions for every city block: where is a public restroom needed, where can one go, and where should it go? It speeds up the desk-review stage of siting; site visits and agency approvals come after it.

Who this is for

Local Law 58 of 2025 requires the office the mayor designates, working with City Planning, Parks and DOT, to deliver a strategic plan for at least 2,120 public restrooms by 2035. The first report was due 1 September 2026; in August the Deputy Mayor's office told the Council it would come by 1 November 2026. The law names the siting factors (population density, foot traffic, transit, walking distance, land use and equity) but not how to weigh them. FLUSHING is built to answer what the plan has to contain:

Local Law 58 asks the plan forWhere FLUSHING answers it
Underserved areas by density, foot traffic, transit, walking distance, land use and equityNeed tiers (Map), City view
Recommended site types, with yields and challengesLand rule, desk review, suggested type, the 30-site list
Legislative, zoning, regulatory or policy changesZoning & BIDs lens
A strategy for keeping restrooms clean and runningMaintenance & contracts lens
Restrooms near transit and micromobility hubsCo-location lens; subway restrooms in the Coverage lens
A public map of existing and planned restrooms, kept currentCoverage lens; "Refresh restrooms"; this one-file map

How we built this

  1. September 2026: three questions. Our scoping memo asked where a public restroom is needed, where one can go, and where it should go.
  2. September: one map for everyone. An urban-management expert asked for a map that works the same way in every district but lets each user set their own priorities.
  3. Early October: a first version. It blended usage, distance, residents and harm into one score. It worked, but nobody could say which factor drove a site, and it did not check whether a unit could stand there.
  4. October 16: city agency interviews. Staff described how DOT sorts streets into demand tiers, and every check a modular restroom site went through before approval. They were clear that no map replaces a site visit.
  5. Now. Each block takes its highest factor, as DOT staff described their demand map; each pick gets a desk review; and a fixed list of 30 candidates is ready for site visits.

The name

FLUSHING spells out what the tool weighs, in order: Foot traffic, Land, Underserved (distance to an open restroom), Site check, Human need (vulnerable residents), Income (poverty), Nuisance (311 public-urination complaints) and Grade (the need tier). It is also a nod to Flushing, Queens: its community district has more residents beyond a 10-minute walk of a restroom than all of Manhattan.

How to use it

  1. Find a place. Search an address, use your location, or pick a district. The list starts with Community District 1 in each borough.
  2. Read the map. "Need tier" shades each block from served to tier 5. "Walk time" shows who can reach a restroom today.
  3. Click a block. "What this means" says its tier, the factor that set it, and its site check. "Show the math" has every step.
  4. Try a scenario. Winter, evening, accessible restrooms only, a different land choice, or other tier thresholds.
  5. Press "Pick sites", or "Show all 30 sites" for the list in our memo. Every pick still needs a site visit.
  6. Add the rest of the city under "Districts and your own data" (about a minute each, with internet), then save "This tool, with my districts".

What is inside

  • 17 districts built in. Six in Manhattan, four in the Bronx, four in Brooklyn, two in Queens and one in Staten Island. Fourteen are the districts where the city placed its 17 Throne restrooms (marked *), built in as a baseline to compare with; three have no Throne unit and are there for contrast: Lower Manhattan, Midtown and Mott Haven. Add them, or any of the other districts, under "Districts and your own data". Built-in ones appear at once; the rest take about a minute with internet.
  • Any area you draw. A boundary file of your own (GeoJSON or .shp), such as a council district or business improvement district, is built the same way.
  • Your own restrooms. Click the map to add one, import a list, or click an existing restroom to stop counting it.
  • Exports. Block results save as CSV or GeoJSON for QGIS, ArcGIS or Excel.

The ideas behind it

  • Simple and explainable. Like DOT's Pedestrian Demand Map, each block takes its highest single factor; nothing is weighted and summed.
  • Access comes first. A block with an open restroom within 5 minutes is served, however busy it is.
  • Peak demand. As DOT designs streets for peak use, tiers assume a typical busy day; winter and evening are optional tests.
  • Desk review, then the ground. Informed by city agency siting processes: physical checks, then approvals by DOT, Parks, MTA, City Hall, the Public Design Commission and community boards. The tool checks what data can show and lists the rest for a site visit.
  • Every step is shown. Each block shows its factors, every source is listed, and what is not known is on the Unknowns page.

Related work

Bathroom Deserts maps how well New Yorkers can reach a usable restroom along walking routes, at different times of day and under different rules for who can get in. It measures access. FLUSHING asks a different question: where to add the next restroom, whether it can stand there, and what its contract should cover. The two can be read together.

What it costs to keep

Hosting is close to free: the tool is one static file that can sit on GitHub Pages or nyc.gov. The real cost is people. About half an analyst's time (about $60,000 a year in the memo) would refresh the restroom list and 311 complaints each quarter, rebuild ACS and PLUTO each year, and add districts. A named city owner is needed when the lab ends.

What changed in v4

  • Six lenses on one map: Siting, Coverage, Evening & winter, Zoning & BIDs, Maintenance & contracts, Co-location & contacts. The view and the letters stay put.
  • A Numbers page with the source and status of every constant, and a sensitivity test.
  • Corrected: DOT's subway rule is 50,000 riders a week, not a day (offered as a preset). Detour factor is now a setting.
  • Every block lists who to contact (community board, council member, BID) and nearby public uses; the site check reads zoning and DOT's automatic-toilet zoning rule.
  • Site profiles for Phase 2 visits, a BID shortlist and a contact sheet can be saved.

What changed in v4.1

  • DOT's subway rule is now the default (50,000 riders a week makes a Regional street). The memo's 30 sites do not change; 46 of 5,635 ranked blocks move up one tier. v3's cut-offs are a preset.
  • Statements that FLUSHING works "the way DOT does" now say where that comes from: DOT staff's description in our interview. The distance step is ours.
  • The city's restroom list of 1 Oct 2026 now supplies changing stations, all-gender rooms, status and notes. The Coverage lens can require them.
  • Fix first: a shortlist of existing restrooms that would bring the most residents within reach if reopened, kept open all year, made accessible or given later hours.
  • The BID shortlist can be limited to commercial districts and ranked three ways. tests/make_shortlists.js saves every shortlist as CSV.

One file

The whole tool is this one HTML file, about 3 MB. It opens in any browser with no internet, login or installation. Internet is only needed to add a district that is not already inside.

Method

A need tier is FLUSHING's 1-to-5 rating of how badly a block needs a public restroom (5 is the greatest need). It takes three steps. Taking the highest factor follows DOT's Pedestrian Demand Map as DOT staff described it to us (E. Doyle, 16 Oct 2026); the distance step is ours.

  1. Distance first.An open restroom within a 5-minute walk: served, not ranked. 5 to 10 minutes: partly served, tier lowered by one. Beyond 10: a gap.
  2. Each factor sets a tier.Foot traffic, vulnerable residents, poverty and public-urination complaints, each from 1 to 5 by the thresholds on the Map page.
  3. Highest tier wins.The block takes its strongest factor, which is shown as the deciding factor. Nothing is weighted or added.

Ties are broken by people on foot, then residents. Land and cost are kept out of the tier: land decides where a unit may stand, and visits and cost feed the contract.

PovertyAbout 53% below the poverty line (census tract)Rating 5

TierHighest ratingTier 5, set by poverty

Reading the tiers

Default thresholds

FactorTier 12345
Foot traffic: DOT street classBaselineCommunityNeighborhoodRegionalGlobal

Vulnerable residents: share 65+, under 5 or with a disabilitybelow 20%20%25%30%35%

Cut-offs are round numbers, the same in every district, so a tier means the same thing everywhere. Resident factors count only on blocks with 10 or more residents, since survey shares come from the surrounding Census tract. A block within a 10-minute walk of a homeless drop-in centre counts as at least tier 4 for vulnerable residents. Ties go to more people on foot, then more residents. Choose a preset or edit a threshold under "Tier thresholds" on the Map page; the 30-site list and the Throne check always use these defaults.

The 30 sites to consider

"Show the next 30 sites" is a fixed reference list on the default settings: one unit in each of the 17 loaded districts, then a second in the 13 districts whose next-best block ranks highest, with public land or a parking space allowed. The allocation is our choice, not part of the method. It is a shortlist for site visits, not a decision.

How sites are picked

"Pick sites" follows the same five rules every time.

  1. Score every block with the settings on the Map page.
  2. Take the block with the highest tier, and among equals the most people on foot.
  3. Find land. If that block passes the Land rule chosen under L, the unit goes there. If not, it goes to the nearest block within 200 m that does. If there is none, the block is listed and the tool moves on.
  4. Count the new unit as built and sort every block again. Blocks near it become served, so the next pick lands somewhere else.
  5. Repeat until the number of sites asked for is reached, or no block is left with a gap.
  6. Check each pick at the desk: land owner, sidewalk clear path, flood plain, who must approve and what kind of restroom fits; then list what needs a site visit (sun, curb uses, below-grade structures, lighting).

Your sites

Your settings

What your choices on the Map page change in this district, compared with the defaults. Click a block on the map to see its arithmetic here too.

Choices made for fairness

  • Access comes firstA block with a restroom nearby is served, however busy it is.
  • One strong factor is enoughA block with heavy foot traffic, or many older residents, or high poverty, rises on that alone, as DOT's map lets one strong generator set a street's class.
  • The walk is timed for a slower walkerTen minutes is farther for a brisk adult than for an older person or a parent with a small child.
  • Land and cost do not lower needNeighbourhoods with little parkland are often the ones with the least access.
  • Small areas are steadiedSurvey figures from an area with few residents are blended with the district average.
  • Complaints are one factor among fourThey show who reports as much as what happens. Arrest data is not used.

Throne check

In September 2026 the city announced 17 Throne restrooms. With those units left out, does FLUSHING see need where the city put them, and more than chance would?

Four tests, each compared with every block in the same districts. The thresholds were not adjusted to fit these sites, and the city chose them by similar logic, so agreement is a sense check, not proof. The tables follow your settings on the Map page.

Unknowns

The tool has no count of who actually needs a restroom where. Each piece is estimated as below. Use the tiers to screen places, then check them on foot.

What it needsHow it guessesWhat that misses
People on footThe city sorts streets into five classes. Each class is given the middle value of the city's pedestrian counts for it: 14,762, 7,327, 4,973, 779 and 390 a day. Subway entries within 400 m, shared among nearby blocks, are used if larger.Bus riders, visitors and street workers. Quiet streets have almost no counts behind them.
Visits a day (contracts only)A flat 1% of people on foot, capped at 120 uses a day for one unit. Not used for tiers.The 1% is an assumption; the cap is near the busiest Throne unit in Long Beach, California (119 a day). Throne's New York counts should replace both.
Walk timeStraight-line distance × 1.3, at 64 metres a minute.The real route: highways, rail lines, large blocks and bridges.
Who has nowhere to goNobody within 5 minutes of a restroom, everybody beyond 10, and a straight line in between.Restrooms that are listed as open but locked, or that need a phone to enter.
Greater needCensus shares for the people who live in the area, applied to the people walking through it.People without a home address, beyond the area around the city's nine drop-in centres. Shelter addresses are not published. Business districts, where residents and passers-by differ.
Poverty and complaintsPoverty share and yearly public-urination complaints within 200 m, each tiered on its own.Places where people do not call 311.
ThresholdsDOT's street classes; DOT's subway rule (more than 50,000 riders a week, about 7,100 a day, makes a Regional street); round numbers for the resident and poverty shares.Cut-offs are a policy choice. The presets show how much they matter: designing for residents or for passers-by changes the list.
Equal tiersA tier 5 from poverty and a tier 5 from foot traffic rank the same.They are different kinds of need. The deciding factor is always shown so readers can see which applies.
Fixed rulesPartly served (5 to 10 minutes) lowers a tier by one; a drop-in centre within 800 m in a straight line (about 16 minutes by the tool's own walk rule, not 10) sets at least tier 4; resident factors need 10 or more residents; a subway station counts within 150 m and complaints within 200 m.Each is a judgement call, written down so it can be tested and changed.
Site checkLand owner, sidewalk width, flood plain, nearness to a subway station and parkland, from city data.Sun for the solar panel, tree lines and setbacks, bus stops and other curb uses that cannot move, structures below grade, lighting. These need a site visit.
Public landOwner names and types in the city's tax-lot records, plus park and plaza outlines.Setbacks from hydrants, trees and entrances; bus stops and loading zones in the curb lane. Sidewalk width is measured from the city's planimetric data, not surveyed.
Other restroomsOnly restrooms in the city's Public Restrooms list: parks, libraries, transit, plazas and privately owned public spaces.Restrooms in cafés, stores, hotels and malls, which many people use. Commercial districts may look needier than they are.
Throne sitesPlaced at the named intersection, or at the centre of the named park or plaza.The exact spot inside a park, which has not been published, and whether each unit is open yet.

Numbers: where each one comes from

Every number in the formula, where it comes from, and whether a sceptical reader could check it.

Sourced from a published source. Derived from data or maths, to be rerun. Our choice a judgement, stated so it can be changed. Assumption or Corrected: weakest, or fixed in v4.

NumberValueStatusWhere it comes from

ServedWithin 5 minutes (half the standard)Our choiceMatches the Council's 5-minute measure. 5 to 10 minutes lowers the tier by one.
Walking speed64 m a minuteSourced3.5 ft a second, the pedestrian speed US signal timing uses (MUTCD section 4E.06). An average adult walks about 80. source
Detour factor1.3 × straight lineDerived, untestedOn a perfect street grid the walk averages 4/π ≈ 1.27 × the straight line over all directions; 1.3 rounds up for superblocks, highways and rail. Not yet checked against routed NYC walks. Test below.
Open water60 m blocks a walkOur choiceStops a straight line from crossing a river or harbour.
Street class → ratingBaseline 1 … Global 5Sourced, numbering oursDOT's five categories from the Pedestrian Demand Map; mapping them to 1–5 is ours. source
People on foot per class14,762 / 7,327 / 4,973 / 779 / 390 a dayDerived, script missingMedian of DOT Bi-Annual Pedestrian Counts (May and Oct 2025) at 74 count sites matched to a class. Used only for ties and visit estimates. The script that made them is not in the repo yet. source
Subway ruleAny station within 150 m → 3; more than 7,143 entries a day → 4SourcedDOT's methodology: a station with more than 50,000 average weekly riders (January 2020) makes a Regional street (rated 4), about 7,143 a day; any other station street is Neighborhood (3). v4.1 makes this the default. v3's own cut-offs (20,000 / 50,000 / 100,000 a day → 3 / 4 / 5) are a preset; switching between them leaves the memo's 30 sites unchanged and moves 46 of 5,635 ranked blocks up one tier. source
Subway distance150 mOur choiceA station this close sets the block's foot-traffic rating.
Vulnerable residents20 / 25 / 30 / 35%Our choiceRound numbers. In the 17 districts the median block is 25.9%, so a typical block already rates 3; 13% of residential blocks reach 5.
Poverty10 / 15 / 20 / 30%Our choiceRound numbers. Median block 14.7%; 19% of residential blocks reach 5, against 6% of blocks for foot traffic.
Complaints1 / 2 / 3 / 5 a year within 200 mOur choiceOne complaint a year already rates 2. 311 shows who calls as much as what happens. source

MTA reviewWithin 100 m of a stationOur choiceFlags structures below grade for a site visit.
Site may moveUp to 200 m to allowed landOur choice
Share of passers-by who need a restroom1%AssumptionNo source. Used for visits and cost only. Replace with Throne's NYC door counts.
Uses one unit can serve120 a daySourcedThe busiest Long Beach Throne averaged 119 a day; its busiest single day was 231. source
Yearly cost per unit$235,000SourcedThrone pilot: $4M for 17 units for one year, service included (NYCEDC). source

How much each number matters

Change one number at a time and see how many residents fall outside a 10-minute walk, how many blocks reach tier 5, and whether the first five sites stay the same. Runs on the district open on the Map page.

How to check our work

  1. Every rule is in one function, calc(), in this file. The Method page follows it line by line.
  2. Click any block and open "Show the math" for its arithmetic.
  3. The memo's 30 sites always use these defaults: "Show the next 30 sites" on the Map page should match Appendix C.
  4. Rebuild steps and every download are in final_prototypes/README.md and data/01_downloads/MANIFEST.md.

Still to do: route real walks on a sample of blocks to test 1.3; add the pedestrian-count script; blend small tracts toward the citywide average.

For developers

The tool is one HTML file with no build step and no dependencies. Everything below works offline except the two network calls marked.

HookupFormatNotes
Import restroomsCSV with latitude/lat/y and longitude/lon/lng/x columns, and an optional column containing name. Or GeoJSON Points (WGS84) with properties.name.Points more than 1.3 km outside the district are skipped. Stored in this browser.
BoundaryGeoJSON Polygon or MultiPolygon (WGS84), or a .shp file in WGS84 (unzipped).Builds a district from open data. Needs internet.
Refresh restroomsSocrata i7jb-7jkuReplaces the current district's restroom list. Needs internet.
Block resultsCSV or GeoJSON, one row or feature per census blockFields: block, address, residents, walk_min, access, nearest, people_on_foot, uses_per_day, gap_share, added_uses, tier, deciding_factor, foot_traffic_tier, residents_tier, poverty_tier, complaints_tier, subway_entries_nearby, vulnerable_share, suggested_type, cost_per_added_use, land, land_owner, sidewalk_ft, near_dropin, land_passes, flood_plain, suggested_site, lon, lat. Reflects the current settings.
District packJSON, version 3o origin [lon, lat]; all shapes are flat [x0, y0, x1, y1, …] rings in metres east and north of it. blocks[]: id census block GEOID, pop, c centre, g rings, s65 s5 sd pv tract shares, pd street class 1–5, tr subway entries, wr winter ratio, c3 yearly 311 complaints, lt land tier 0–3, fl flood plain, sw sidewalk ft, di near a drop-in centre. Also rest, user, off, st, dc, parks, plazas, cd, land, lab.
This tool, with my districtsHTMLA copy of this file with every district and edit inside it, for sharing.

Open-data calls made by the builder: Socrata 5crt-au7u, fwpa-qxaf, erm2-nwe9, bmxf-3rd4, 64uk-42ks, enfh-gkve, k5k6-6jex, i7jb-7jku on data.cityofnewyork.us; Census TIGERweb blocks; Esri Living Atlas ACS layers. Subway ridership is stored in the file.

Still needed

  • Use counts and exact locations for the NYC Throne units.
  • Bus boardings and fuller foot-traffic data.
  • Actual restroom opening hours. The City Council found 1 in 9 park restrooms closed during posted hours.
  • Curb uses: bus stops, hydrants and loading zones.
  • Sidewalk widths for districts built in the browser.
